Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse’s Complete Relationship Timeline

📅 2019-08-23  |  Read Source →

Despite Robert Pattinson’s big-screen career and Suki Waterhouse’s supermodel status, the public doesn’t know much about their relationship. Both of these Brits prefer to keep their private lives out of the public sphere. As their romance continues past the five-year mark and the couple settles into parenthood, here’s a rundown of their secretive story.

Pattinson and Waterhouse were first linked on July 30 when E! obtained photos of the pair kissing in the streets of London. Per the outlet’s report, the two saw a 9 P.M. showing of Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again at Electric Cinema in Notting Hill. They then walked across the street for drinks at SoHo House until 1 A.M.An eyewitness said the couple was open with their affection. “Along the way, they were very close and cuddled and kissed many times,” the source told E! News. “Robert was very affectionate to her and had his arm around her the whole way and Suki reciprocated by holding his hand and kissing it. They were very loved up and close. Robert stroked Suki’s hair and gave her another loving kiss.”

An E! source said the pair was only “casually dating.” Since Pattinson had only recently ended a three-year relationship, “he isn’t looking for anything serious right now.”

The insider did express that the two “are definitely into each other” and are dating while Pattinson is in London filming The King. “Rob likes to have fun when he has breaks in-between filming and him and Suki have a great time together,” the source added.

LaineyGossip disputed breakup rumors that surfaced at the time, sharing that Pattinson had FaceTimed Waterhouse walking home from a London pub in August. Per the outlet’s report, the couple was spotted at Miguel’s concert in Los Angeles.

They each also attended the Toronto International Film Festival for their own projects that month. Pattinson was promoting High Life while Waterhouse walked the carpet for Assassination Nation.

The couple was photographed exiting London club Chiltern Firehouse at 2:15 A.M., seemingly confirming they were still together.

Photos surfaced of the couple leaving a Christmas party on London’s Regent Street. Waterhouse and Pattinson stayed at the party until the early morning hours.

Waterhouse and Pattinson spent her 27th birthday together, photographed leaving her party. A couple weeks later, People ran photos of them holding hands after a run in London.

Pattinson made his first public comments about his relationship with Waterhouse.

The Sunday Times asked Pattinson about Waterhouse, and he responded by asking, “Do I have to [talk about her]?” Then he went into more detail about why he’s so private about his personal life:

“If you let people in, it devalues what love is. If a stranger on the street asked you about your relationship, you’d think it extremely rude. If you put up a wall it ends up better. I can’t understand how someone can walk down the street holding hands, and it’s the same as when I do it and a hundred people are taking your photo. The line between when you’re performing and when you’re not will eventually get washed away, and you’ll go completely mad.”

However, he did tell the outlet that breakups with Kristen Stewart and FKA Twigs didn’t disillusion him to romance with a celebrity. “They were pretty long relationships, not like three months.”

When it came time for Pattinson’s 33rd birthday, he and Waterhouse were photographed at Chateau Marmont. Pattinson’s friend Tom Sturridge was also in attendance for the celebrations, per People.

During a June interview with Grazia, the reporter noted that Waterhouse FaceTimed Pattinson during a photo shoot break.

E! published a picture of Pattinson and Waterhouse strolling through London as they marked one year of dating.

In early September, photographer Sofia Malamute shared a photo of the couple cuddled together, captioned, “Ibiza, 2019.”

After several months of staying out of the public eye, Waterhouse and Pattinson confirmed their relationship was still going strong. The pair was seen leaving Waterhouse’s 27th birthday party in London on January 12, per LaineyGossip.

They celebrated her birthday at London’s Casa Cruz, and attendees included Liv Tyler, Georgia May Jagger, Cara Delevingne, and Ashley Benson.

Pattinson essentially confirmed that he was quarantining with Waterhouse during an interview for GQ’s June cover. According to the article, Pattinson had been sequestered “with his girlfriend” in the London apartment “the Batman folks rented for him” while production on the film was paused.

The couple signaled they were still going strong, two years into their relationship, with a pair of public outings. On July 21, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed walking arm-in-arm around London’s Notting Hill.

A source spoke to E! about the sighting, telling the outlet, “They weren’t recognized by anyone and they seemed to be in their own little world as they took a long stroll around the village chatting intently, pointing at properties and laughing together before they arrived at the club. They held hands the whole time or were linking arms and looked very happy.”

The following day, People published another photo of the couple on a walk. An insider told the outlet, “They are very loved-up,” adding, “they haven’t been together that long. But everything seems on the fast track. They are always laughing and smiling at each other.”

The pair’s most PDA-filled photo yet arrived about 12 days after Pattinson was reported to have tested positive for COVID-19, per CBS News. Although the studio never confirmed that report, production on The Batman was “temporarily paused.” It resumed in September, days after Pattinson and Waterhouse’s outing. In the photo, the couple sat on a London park bench with coffees, kissing while their masks were pulled down to their chins.

Pattinson’s recovery apparently only strengthened his relationship. A source told E! that “Rob and Suki have definitely discussed getting engaged but are in no rush. Suki is not pressuring him, and they are both very committed to each other.”

The insider confirmed the couple’s romance is “stronger than ever” after quarantine. “They love being low-key together and have very similar interests,” the source added. “They are truly inseparable and in love.”

Shortly after E! reported the two had discussed getting engaged, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed out with Pattinson’s parents in London. The two walked side-by-side behind Pattinson’s mom and dad on November 23. They opted not to show any PDA in front of them or the photographers who captured this outing.

After months out of the limelight, Waterhouse made headlines when she posted a selfie of herself on April 15. Eagle-eyed fans noticed that a photo of her kissing Pattinson was visible in the background.

On April 19, Pattinson and Waterhouse were photographed out in London for the first time in 2021. The two held hands while walking in Notting Hill. Both dressed casually, wearing shorts and hoodies. It served as a rare public signal that a year into quarantine, the couple’s relationship remained strong.

Waterhouse called out the HBO Max Gossip Girl reboot for making a joke at her expense. The joke in question: Teen public relations whiz Luna (Zión Moreno) is trying to talk Zoya (Whitney Peak) into stepping up her influencer game. She says, “When are you going to get it? As far as the press is concerned, he’s R-Patz, and you’re Suki Nobody.”

In a now-deleted series of tweets, Waterhouse responded with the following: “Another day to be reminded that women can also be the patriarchy. Seeing critiques of patriarchy and sexism, then I get name-checked as somebody’s ‘nobody’ girlfriend,” per Glamour.

Some fans compared Waterhouse’s response to Taylor Swift’s tweet about Netflix’s Ginny & Georgia’s joke about her.

“Hey Ginny & Georgia, 2010 called and it wants its lazy, deeply sexist joke back. How about we stop degrading hard working women by defining this horse shit as FuNnY,” she wrote. “Also, @netflix after Miss Americana this outfit doesn’t look cute on you Happy Women’s History Month I guess.”

A source gave E! a rare and brief update on how Waterhouse and Pattinson were doing three years into dating: great, naturally.

“They are very solid in their relationship,” the source said. During the rare public appearances they do together, they’re “always just totally joined at the hip. You can tell he’s completely in love with her,” the source said.

Ahead of the holidays, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed on December 8 holding hands in New York City on a winter day date. Pattinson wore a monochrome blue look consisting of a hooded puffer jacket with matching blue pants. Waterhouse chose earth tones, stepping out in a brown Carhartt hat, rose-colored wool coat, and a black Dior cashmere shawl. It was their first time being photographed out together in months.

Pattinson opened up a little about his life with Waterhouse in two interviews during his The Batman press tour.

To GQ, he spoke about her impact on his decision-making—and how she trolled him by talking with a repairman at their place about DC Comics.

Pattinson said Waterhouse was the reason why he changed the location for his GQ interview from the London Zoo to Holland Park. “I was talking to my girlfriend last night and she was, like, ‘You know, people don’t really like zoos.…’” he said. “I’d been thinking about a metaphorical thing. But then I was thinking that’s very wrong, a sad bear walking in circles. I just can’t help it. I’ll do it for every single element, every decision, in my life. What is the worst-case scenario for this decision?”

And with the repairman for their place’s boiler, “The guy came around the other day, and he just randomly started talking about what a DC [Comics] fan he is. And I’m sitting there facing the other direction, and my girlfriend just keeps continuing the conversation with him. And I’m looking at her like: Shut the fuck up!” He laughed. “Why are you doing this to me? She was very entertaining. Just talking to an obsessive fan.”

Pattinson later talked on Jimmy Kimmel Live! about Waterhouse’s emotional reaction watching The Batman and how it made him more terrified of its release. “It was really her reaction that kind of changed the entire thing because I’m pretty sure she’s not normally into watching superhero movies,” he said, via Entertainment Tonight. “And just seeing that it was capturing her attention the entire time and then she held my hand and touched it [to her face] and I could feel a little tear. And I was like, ‘No way!’”

On Friday, May 6, the couple was spotted in Los Angeles after Waterhouse’s show at The Echo. She was touring to promote her new album, I Can’t Let Go. Pattinson was in a baseball cap and mask to keep a low profile. He was wearing a black jacket, gray T-shirt, and a pair of jeans with sneakers. His girlfriend was in jeans and a colorful long-sleeve shirt over a sparkling top. She had on a pair of black boots with a chunky heel.

They walked down the street as Waterhouse spoke into her phone, and Pattinson threw a casual arm around her waist. She responded with an embrace, continuing her conversation as they went.

Pattinson and Waterhouse made their red carpet debut in Giza, Egypt, while attending the Dior fall 2023 menswear show. As the couple posed for the cameras, they giggled and flirted with one another like they were on their first date.

Later that month, on December 28, the couple was seen making their way through JFK like many holiday travelers. Waterhouse had a few bags over her shoulders, but Pattinson was pushing the majority of their luggage from the trip on a cart, with a guitar slung across his back.

Waterhouse and Pattinson started the new year together. People reported that the two threw a New Year’s Eve party at the Moxy Hotel on New York City’s Lower East Side. A source told the outlet, “Rob and Suki had a great time. He had a table in the corner and was laughing a lot. He and Suki were by each other’s side the entire night. It was a fun evening.”

The Times published an interview with Waterhouse, where she spoke more openly about their relationship than ever before. The outlet revealed they live in London together. “I’m shocked that I’m so happy with someone for nearly five years,” Waterhouse said, noting that they don’t really spend long apart.

On whether they give each other acting advice, she said, “Rob definitely isn’t getting advice from me about acting, but of course I’ll try and get him to help me with an audition before he falls asleep on the sofa.”

Communication makes their relationship work, she added: “I’m always incredibly excited when I see his name pop up [on my phone] or even a text, and I think he feels the same about me,” she said. “We’ve always got so much to say, and I find him hilarious.”

The two both grew up in southwest London and marvel over the fact they ended up together, with such similar journeys in the entertainment industry. “We always say that I never, ever would have thought I’d go out with a boy from Barnes, and he didn’t think he’d go out with a girl from Chiswick,” Waterhouse said.

She didn’t address her future plans with Pattinson explicitly but did say generally she hopes to start a family someday. “You have to be like, ‘I’m going be a sitting cow for a bit of time,’ but it’s going to be worth it,” she said of having children. “I can’t wait. I wish you could click your fingers to make it happen.”

Waterhouse appeared in an interview on CBS Mornings to discuss how she prepared to play keyboardist Karen Sirko in the new Amazon Prime Video series Daisy Jones & The Six. It involved lots of practicing that she said Pattinson had to sit through in their new home.

“Did he enjoy that? Yeah, probably not,” she joked about the practice sessions. But she added that he has his own musical abilities—the actor performed two songs on the Twilight soundtrack, with credits for co-writing “Let Me Sign.”

“He’s actually way worse at being annoying about—well, because he’s an amazing pianist and a really great guitarist,” Waterhouse explained. “He’s amazing, honestly.”

He apparently plays his music for her a lot, and she quipped, “He wins the annoying competition.”

Pattinson and Waterhouse made their Met Gala debut, posing on the red carpet alongside each other:

Waterhouse and Pattinson signaled once more that all is going well between them when they were photographed holding hands while out for a walk in New York City on July 30.

On Saturday, October 21, Waterhouse and Pattinson attended the GO Campaign’s annual gala in Los Angeles. Waterhouse wore a sheer burgundy dress that showed her matching bra and underwear beneath, and Pattinson had on a black suit with a black button-down shirt.

Inside, photos showed them at their table with Waterhouse wearing his blazer over her shoulders. The nonprofit GO raises money for orphans worldwide, and Pattinson is one of their ambassadors.

The pair was photographed on a hike in Los Angeles on November 1. She wore a loose navy sweater with gray shorts, while he was in a gray hoodie and shorts.

On Friday, November 10, the couple went on another hike in Los Angeles. The actress wore a cropped black T-shirt and matching leggings with a black baseball cap. Pattinson wore a weighted hiking vest with shorts and a pair of Adidas sneakers.

On November 19, Waterhouse confirmed pregnancy rumors at the time while performing at Mexico’s Corona Festival. In footage shared on social media, the artist appears in a sparkly, form-fitting minidress with her pregnant stomach visible. She told the audience, “I thought I’d wear something sparkly to distract you from something else I’ve got going on... I’m not sure it’s working.” This was both Waterhouse and Pattinson’s first child.

On November 20, Waterhouse made her pregnancy Instagram official with a mirror selfie.

Waterhouse and Pattinson sparked engagement rumors when Waterhouse was photographed wearing a toi et moi diamond ring on her left ring finger. See photos here.

Since revealing her pregnancy, Waterhouse posted several carousels of pictures from that time of her life. A few days before Christmas, she shared photos from what looks like a tropical vacation, standing in a floral string bikini with a scarf wrapped around her head. In another pic, she had on a crop top showing a peek at her midriff and in yet another, she wore a black-and-white shirt and shorts set with a red handkerchief top underneath that revealed her belly.

The next day, she shared a bunch of photos of what looks like her holiday outfit, a gown by Di Petsa, made of a semi-sheer mesh material that created a “wet look” that was sculpted around her torso.

On December 6, they were seen out in New York City with Taylor Swift.

The couple confirmed they welcomed their first child in late March when they were photographed out walking in Los Angeles. Pattinson pushed their baby in a stroller, while Waterhouse appeared visibly not pregnant in a black coat. The pair had not shared their child’s name, birth date, or sex.

Waterhouse shared the first photo of her and Pattinson’s baby on Instagram. She opted not to share any additional details, including the baby’s sex or name. “welcome to the world angel ❤️,” she wrote.

On April 12, Waterhouse performed at the 2024 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival and revealed on stage that the new baby is a girl.

“I don’t know if some of you know, but I had some big life changes happen recently, some pretty big events have been going down,” she told the audience. “I love amazing ladies, and I’ve been very lucky to have my own little amazing lady and meet the love of my life.”

That same night, she and Pattinson were seen at the festival together walking around the Empire Polo Field, enjoying the event. The Twilight star wore a yellow graphic T-shirt, a gold chain, gray pants, and a black baseball cap. Waterhouse was dressed in a furry white wrap, shorts, and sheer black tights.

On April 21, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed on a walk with their daughter in Los Angeles. Pattinson pushed the stroller, while Waterhouse was beside him in an oversize white T-shirt, gray sweatpants, and a dark gray sweater.

On Friday, May 31, Waterhouse and Pattinson enjoyed a date night at Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles. The model wore a white top and high-waisted jeans under a black leather biker jacket. She carried a black bag with stud details and wore a pair of espadrille loafers. Pattinson wore a graphic print T-shirt and brown leather jacket with black jeans and sneakers.

Later in the month, Pattinson made his way to Paris for the Dior Homme Menswear Spring/Summer 2025 Show. Fans posted a clip of him talking to a reporter about his daughter for the first time.

“[Having a child] makes you feel very old and very young,” he said, adding, “She’s so cute. And you know, I’m amazed by how quickly their personality comes. So even at three months, I’m like, ‘Oh…I can kinda see who she is already.’”

He also shared he only planned to be in Paris for one day so he could return to his family.

Waterhouse spoke to British Vogue about her life with Pattinson and their daughter, along with how the couple met six years before at a games night in L.A. “I was sure that I’d met him a long time ago, but he didn’t think that we had,” she prefaced. They played a game called Werewolf that was “very, very intense. There were lots of ‘big’ characters, real heavy hitters [in the room]. Al Pacino was there. Javier and Penelope were there…and, you know, everyone was really acting.”

She and Pattinson, “I think we both sort of have the same slight uncomfortable-ness [and quickly] started giggling at the absurdity of the whole thing,” she said, adding they “got told off” for being so disruptive. “There was a director that separated us because we were laughing too much.”

They met again “six or seven months” later, Waterhouse said, and that meeting endeared her more to him. She remembered thinking, “I think Rob’s quite funny, I light up when I’m around him. [Living in L.A.] definitely became a lot more fun when I met him.”

She shared they really planned their pregnancy years later: “One day we looked at each other and said, ‘Well, this is as ready as we’re going to be.’”

Pattinson made her a rap playlist for her birth. “He was there with me and like all dads, he was really nervous, but for someone who’s quite an anxious person, he’s been very calm,” she said. “[He’s] the dad I could have hoped for. I mean a dad and his daughter? It’s an actual love story.”

She also shared he isn’t bothered at all by her exes or them reaching out about the music she makes. “He couldn’t really give a shit,” she said. “He’s like, ‘No one’s better than me, so whatever.’” Overall, she called her life with him and their baby her “dream.”

On Friday, August 9, the couple enjoyed a date night at celebrity hotspot Chiltern Firehouse in London. Waterhouse wore a semi-sheer look with a frilled pink top and translucent black pants. She was photographed leaving the venue in a long black coat with fluffy fur lapels. She left her hair down and accessorized with yellow heels. Pattinson was wearing a blue sweatshirt, khaki pants, a black jacket, and a baseball cap and sneakers.

The two parents enjoyed a walk with their daughter on September 24 in Los Angeles. Both wore black and tan outfits. Pattinson was in a dark hoodie and khaki shorts. Waterhouse had on a leather jacket and longer light tan pants. See photos of them here.

The couple made their first official appearance together since welcoming their daughter on October 5 at the Veuve Clicquot Polo Classic at Will Rogers State Historic Park. Waterhouse wore a black dress with a floral pattern, puffed sleeves, and a belted waist. Pattinson was in a blue suit and a white button-down shirt. They both wore sunglasses.

On Thanksgiving weekend, Waterhouse and Pattinson were photographed walking with their daughter in a carriage outside La Poubelle restaurant in Los Angeles, holding coffee cups.

The model was wearing a black hoodie and wide-legged jeans with sunglasses. Pattinson was in a white hoodie and gray cargo pants with a trucker hat and sunglasses.

In May, Pattinson headed to the Cannes Film Festival to promote his new film with Jennifer Lawrence, Die My Love. He made a rare comment about fatherhood on the red carpet, saying, “I think, in the most unexpected ways, having a baby gives you the biggest trove of energy and inspiration afterward. It’s a different kind of energy.”

He added, “Ever since she was born, it’s reinvigorated the way I approach work, and yeah, you’re a completely different person the next day.”

On Memorial Day weekend, he was back in Los Angeles and seen pushing his daughter’s stroller down the street after grabbing a cup of coffee.

On November 1, Waterhouse joined Pattinson on the red carpet, marking a very rare public appearance together since welcoming their daughter. The couple posed together at the New York premiere of Pattinson’s new film, Die My Love, at AMC Lincoln Center Theater.

They shared a sweet moment in front of photographers and were seen later walking together after the screening.

In an interview with GQ, Pattinson admitted that before he became a dad, he “wasn’t the biggest fan of kids.”

“I didn’t mind them. I would tolerate them,” he shared, saying that now being with his daughter is “the most fun thing. I think it’s absolutely wonderful.”

“It’s just that everything is time management, the whole time. I mean, it’s kind of obvious, but you don’t realize it until you do it,” he continued. “Even if you’re on the other side of the planet, you’re like, ‘Okay, I cannot spend more than 10 days away.’ After 10 days of being away, it’s physical pain. It’s so interesting, your body chemistry changes without you even thinking about it.”

He was then asked if she had watched his movies, and Pattinson stated she has “seen so many” of his and Waterhouse’s films, joking she was a fan of Mickey-17 over popular kids’ cartoon Cocomelon.

He then joked that he is “not getting any respect.”

“I’ll be like, ‘Who’s this? Who’s that on the screen?’ And she’s like…[blank stare]. And I’m like, ‘It begins with a D! Ends with a Y!’” he laughed.

On March 15, Waterhouse and Pattinson stepped out for a date night at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party in Los Angeles. Pattinson wore a black Dior suit, while Waterhouse opted for an ivory Tamara Ralph gown with a sheer cape and embellished bodice.

Days later on March 17, Waterhouse joined Pattinson at The Drama’s Los Angeles premiere. Pattinson was in Dior, while Waterhouse wore a Harris Reed dress.

In a May 28 interview with Variety, the actress implied she and Pattinson are considering more kids eventually.

“I feel like I’m in it for the long run,” Waterhouse shared. “I just want to keep creating, really, and maybe have a larger family…like max two more kids. That would be cool.”

During a July 28 appearance on the And The Writer Is... podcast, Waterhouse shared a glimpse into family life, revealing the nickname their daughter gave Pattinson as he films The Batman Part II.

Waterhouse said that their 2-year-old has started recognizing both of her parents’ careers. “She like knows what I do now,” the singer said. “She like points it out in a story book. We were looking at jobs the other day, and she was like, ‘That’s your job, like the girl with the guitar.’”

She added that their daughter has also embraced Pattinson’s latest role, saying, “She calls him ‘Daddy Batman’ now because he’s always dressed up like that now for the next seven months whenever he’s on FaceTime.”

On September 5, Waterhouse joined Pattinson at the premiere of Primetime, marking their first-ever appearance together at the Venice Film Festival. The actress arrived in a Saint Laurent two-piece gold lace set, while Pattinson stood out in a striped white Dior suit. They posed together for photographers:

In an interview with The Times, Waterhouse said that her wedding plans were on hold “at least until this year is over.”

“It would either be all or nothing,” she said, via People. “If we were going to go for it, we’d have a massive party, blow it out.”

On November 2 at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, Waterhouse told E! News that she’s already looking forward to Christmas with Pattinson and their daughter.

“The tradition I’m most looking forward to is just dressing the tree,” she said, before adding that she’s “excited to go back to London and start drinking a lot of mulled wine.” She explained that she, in fact, makes her own mulled wine and gifts it to loved ones. “I go big at Christmas. I’m excited.”

The 9 Best Running Shoes for Runners With Flat Feet and Low Arches

📅 2019-01-08  |  Read Source →

No, you don’t need more arch support. But here’s what you do need.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 6, 2026: Our Best Overall, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is 19% off! Our team is currently testing the Adrenaline GTS 26, which is on sale now.

Shopping for running shoes can be especially frustrating if you have flat feet. There are conflicting opinions about what types of shoes best accommodate your foot shape. Some shoe brands add lots of arch support. Other experts say the opposite. What’s a flat-footed runner to do?

Despite the confusion, there are solutions out there, especially with flat feet being more common than you think. Finding shoes that work with your foot type, support good running form, and feel comfortable is paramount—and totally doable.

Not all flat feet are the same, which means there’s no universal solution that will work well for everyone. We’ll go over what it means to have flat feet and some of the potential issues the condition can present for runners. We’ve also highlighted shoe designs that might help alleviate any pain or discomfort you’re experiencing. Finally, we’ve picked the best running shoes for flat feet you can buy right now, including a wide range of options for walking, speedwork, trail running, and more.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 (Men’s/Women’s)On a budget → New Balance Ellipse (Men’s/Women’s)Searching for some stability → Hoka Arahi 9 (Men’s/Women’s)Adding speedwork to your training → Brooks Ghost Amp (Men’s/Women’s)In need of more cushioned support → Saucony Guide 19 (Men’s/Women’s)Curious about zero-drop → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s)Training to race → New Balance SuperComp Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)Racing a marathon → Hoka Rocket X 3 (unisex)Pavement-averse → Hoka Speedgoat 7 (Men’s/Women’s)

Runner’s World Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer—who has relatively low arches—researched shoe testing data from our team of approximately 300 wear-testers. Our program includes runners of various experience levels, paces, gaits, and, most important for this guide, arch types. They logged hundreds of miles in these shoes, evaluating comfort, fit, and ride.

Our contributors also gathered intel from industry experts. Caitlin Giddings consulted Kimberly Davis, DC, ART, who is CEO and founder of RunLab in Austin, Texas, and physical therapist Jay Dicharry, author of Anatomy for Runners. Both Davis and Dicharry have extensive experience assessing and treating runners of all experience levels, gait types, and footwear needs; they were able to provide significant insight on the topic. Michael Charboneau, former RW editor and freelance reviewer for InsideHook, Men’s Journal, and other publications, also offered his expertise in our Q&A section.

Shop the best flat-footed running shoe deals on Amazon

The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is as much a runner-fave as its neutral counterpart, the Brooks Ghost 18. This updated version of the Adrenaline GTS features even more cushioning. Brooks heightened the forefoot 3 mm and the heel 1 mm, bringing the offset down from 12 mm to 10 mm. This means more of a balanced feel underfoot. The nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam provides a responsive, plush ride for everyday training and long runs.

Tester Peter Vuong, an overpronator with a flat arch, gave his seal of approval.

“This is a solid, all-around shoe with good flexibility, comfort, and a smooth ride,” he said. “I loved my runs in this shoe. It’s comfortable and laces up nice and snug. The fit is near-perfect. I tested it mostly on the road with a little trail. I would use this shoe for many occasions including a 5K race or nice Sunday 10-miler. It’s nice to have something for multiple uses like that.”

The shoe has the brand’s holistic stability guide rails system. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides of the Adrenaline GTS act as “bumpers” to help align the knee and ankle when form gets erratic from overpronating. Testers said the fit and support were spot-on.

“I’ve run in just about every model of this shoe, many of them predating the guide rails system,” said tester Chris Garges. “This shoe provides the stability that I need as a heel-striking overpronator. I had no issues with the stability even later into a 14-mile training run. Some prior Adrenalines and the Glycerin GTS shoes seem to have a touch too much foot movement, particularly in warm, sweaty weather, which causes blisters or loss of toenails. I did not experience those issues with these shoes.”

Think of the new Ellipse as your run club shoe; New Balance’s newest trainer is meant to make running easier with plenty of pop. The midsole is the brand’s Fresh Foam X, which ensures high energy return on your run as well as plenty of high-cushioned support that absorbs shock. It’s also a generous bed of plush for flat feet.

Testers praised the shoe’s cushioning, even though the ride for some felt slightly bulky. It’s not necessarily a speed shoe, but that didn’t stop some of our testers from going fast on that runner’s high. “It truly feels like I am at an advantage wearing these shoes,” said tester Laura Parks.

The dual-density compression-molded EVA midsole is retooled so the ride is even softer and more supportive. Think of the new midsole as a plush bed of comfort for your flat feet.

If you thought choosing to run in a low-drop shoe meant a non-supportive barefoot ride (not the ideal for runners with flat feet), then you’ve never run in the Altra Fwd Via 2. Formerly known for making exclusively zero-drop trainers, Altra has released low-drop shoes these past couple of years, welcoming the zero-drop curious into their fold.

Shoes like the Fwd Via 2 have a 4 mm offset, which is merely the height of two stacked nickels. This low heel-to-toe drop helps runners ease into running in this type of trainer without fully making the plunge to zero drop. The plush cushioning also helps with the low-drop transition. Your arches won’t feel sore due to lack of support thanks to the thick bed of Altra Ego P35 midsole foam, which reaches 37 mm in the heel.

Like all of Altra’s shoes, a wide toebox provides wiggle room. The shoe also has a slight rocker shape to promote propulsion.

Think of the SuperComp Rebel as the successor to the SuperComp Elite v4, New Balance’s premium racing shoe beloved for its accessible features: a broader base, beefier cushioning for marathoners clocking over five hours, a rocker sole and carbon plate that’s propulsive but not too aggressive. The brand made the SuperComp Elite v6 snappier; it’s comparable to the Brooks Hyperion Elite 6. Though the SC Rebel is a “training companion” for longer efforts and carbon-plate conditioning, it’s also race day-worthy.

The midsole is the brand’s Infinion foam, which was featured in the max-cushioned 1080v15. The Infinion foam in the SC Rebel, however, is fine-tuned for springier, faster efforts.

“I enjoyed the energetic bounce I got running in these sneakers,” said tester Nina Rems. “My legs felt light and my feet felt quick. You definitely feel the difference running in sneakers with a carbon plate versus just foam soles. I was more responsive in these New Balance SuperComp Rebels than my regular trainers, New Balance 1080s.”

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

The Rocket X 3 is Hoka-soft with all the super shoe features. The broader base makes this shoe’s fit and ride not as severe as competitors’. Our midfoot didn’t feel squeezed, our toes weren’t crowded, and corner turns didn’t cause our life to flash before our eyes. What you get running in the Rocket X 3 is a stable—but fast—racing experience.

The shoe has dual-density PEBA foam and a winged carbon-fiber plate. Even though its ride is not as aggressive as the brand’s other racing shoe, the Cielo X1 2.0, it still packs a bouncy punch for running half marathons and marathons, and offers plenty of cushioning so your body won’t take a beating hours on the road.

“I love the push-off,” said Erica Bobstein. “They are bouncy and springy and they allow you to propel yourself forward with less effort. They do not have the same speedroll effect as the Saucony Endorphin Pro, but rather have an explosive push-off that requires less energy.”

A combination of plush maximum cushioning and all the tech you need to stay upright on the trail is a winning recipe for flat-footed runners tired of staying on the roads. The Speedgoat gets a reworking with its seventh iteration, resulting in a more secure—albeit, snug for wide feet—fit, and midsole foam that provides comfort for ultra distances.

Toothy lugs provide grip and stability over mixed, technical terrain, while the Meta-Rocker geometry smooths out heel-to-toe transitions. The supercritical EVA foam is tweaked to add more pop on the trail.

Tester Diane Grim, who previously tested the Speedgoat 6, noticed a significant difference in the shoe’s bounce with the 7. She found the ride more forgiving, “which could be great for the long runs, less foot fatigue.”

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Some runners have anatomically flat feet, and other runners have what’s known as “collapsed arches,” which are flat because of a muscle weakness. Although the two types can look very similar, how you approach buying shoes for them varies widely, says Dr. Kimberly Davis of the RunLab, an Austin, Texas-based clinic that assesses running biomechanics and offers physical therapy and training.

Dr. Davis says that when it comes to shopping for a shoe for a flat-footed runner with collapsed arches due to muscle weakness, you can add arch support until the foot gets stronger and can support its own arch. But with an anatomically flat foot, arch support just sends stress up into the knee where it can lead to knee problems.

That’s why it’s important to know what type of flat foot you have before you settle on a shoe—and take into account not just your foot but your entire body, including knees, hips, and range of motion.

Added Arch Support Is Not Always the Answer

Runners with flat feet tend to overpronate, which is when the arches of the foot roll inward after landing. (This isn’t true across the board—there are plenty of flat-footed runners who are biomechanically sound and efficient, and don’t experience any overpronation.)

Up until recently, the running industry steered overpronators toward stability shoes to control this motion. Gradually, all that is starting to change with the realization that stability features don’t do much to correct the natural cycle of the foot, though some runners prefer having them.

Dr. Davis says people with flat feet often have really flexible feet that never get rigid for the push-off. “The footwear industry tries to solve that by putting an arch support in there to give them an arch or create suppination in the foot,” she says. “But that foot is structurally built that way, it’s not something you can solve with a shoe.”

Flat-Footed Runners Can Benefit From a Full-Contact Midsole

Jay Dicharry, author of Anatomy for Runners and director of the REP Lab in Bend, Oregon, agrees arch support can be detrimental because the arch is by nature dynamic, and having extra structure there can stop your foot from moving. Dicharry says flat-footed runners should put more focus on seeking out a shoe with a straight “last,” which is the mold that dictates the shape of the shoe. A straight-lasted shoe has a wider midfoot base and less of a cut-in, a profile that has fallen by the wayside in favor of hourglass-shaped shoes.

Most current shoes don’t provide much of a solid support surface for flat-footed runners, he says. “The problem is all these hourglass shoe shapes look nice on the wall, but when someone with a flat foot puts weight on one, part of their foot is bearing weight on the fabric upper,” he says. “The upper doesn’t work as a midsole for foot support. Feet do well when they’re on an even surface.”

The truth is most running shoes will work for most runners; however, if the shoes you’re using aren’t comfortable immediately or if you’re experiencing any pain while running, you should try a different pair. Get your movement pattern analyzed, whether at a clinic like the RunLab or even a running store that offers gait analysis.

Once you have more information about your feet and movement patterns, you can provide all that information to a running store to find the best shoe for you. Don’t be afraid to take a shoe out for a test run following assessment before purchasing anything.

Here’s a quick way to find out what kind of arches you have: Grab a piece of cardboard and head to the bathroom. Put the cardboard on the floor, wet the bottom of your feet with water in the bathtub or shower, then stand on the cardboard. If you see dry spaces where your arches are, you don’t have flat feet; if you see full footprints showing both soles, then your feet are flat.

As we noted in our explainer, there are multiple kinds of flat feet, and some feet are more flat than others. For a clear, detailed understanding of your foot shape and what kind of foot support you need, you should speak to a podiatrist or running expert.

How can I tell if I have naturally flat feet or collapsed arches?

People with naturally flat feet generally have the condition their entire lives. (Everyone is born with flat feet. Your arches develop in the first few years of life.) Collapsed arches are caused by muscle weakness or an injury. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the most common cause is “inflammation or a tear in the leg tendon (posterior tibial tendon) that supports the arch.”

Both naturally flat feet and collapsed arches can be painful, however, so if you’re experiencing discomfort, it’s best to consult with a doctor to determine which type you have.

My flat feet are causing pain and discomfort. What can I do to alleviate that?

Experts recommend stretching your Achilles, calves, and hamstrings. Stretching those tendons and muscles will help reduce strain on your feet. See our guides to strengthening and stretching the Achilles, calves, and hamstrings for specific exercises.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Michael is a freelance writer with years of experience covering gear and the outdoors for Runner's World and other publications; when he's not writing, he's usually biking, hiking, and running in the mountains around Los Angeles, where he lives.

These Bangkok Hotels Offer In-House Experiences, Beautiful Views, and Excellent Bang for Your Buck

📅 2018-12-13  |  Read Source →

After 14 years in Bangkok, I’ve watched the city evolve into one of the most electric destinations in Southeast Asia. It’s a city of duality—constantly on the move with new hotel openings, world-class restaurants, and an ever-changing shopping scene, but with tradition firmly at its core.

There's something in Bangkok for every kind of traveler, no matter your age or budget. You can enjoy a lunch made by an 80-year-old auntie still serving the same streetside crab omelet she has for decades, or dine at the only three-Michelin-star restaurant in Thailand for dinner. Ancient golden temples stand alongside modern shopping centers, and old shophouses are being revived by the younger generation who want to preserve the city's heritage. When it comes to the hotel scene, this dichotomy is also in play. Guests can choose between historic boutique properties or glamorous new builds, and find every kind of amenity, design style, or cuisine under the sun.

Just as captivating is the warmth and hospitality of the Thai people, something I’ve found to be unlike anywhere else in the world. Thailand is known as the “Land of Smiles,” and from my experience, it more than lives up to its name. The city reveals itself through small, thoughtful moments mixed with grand experiences, all set to an energetic pace that makes it one of my favorite destinations. If you're ready to see it all for yourself, read on for some of the best hotels in Thailand. —Megan Leon

The 30-story tower that this hotel calls home cuts a striking figure in the Bangkok skyline, shaped as it is after the wai, a Thai gesture of greeting made by pressing one’s palms together—a fitting shape for a place that beautifully melds Thai hospitality with a hyper-polished service style. The staff here is supremely gracious: They remember names, press buttons for guests at the elevator banks, turn tables over quickly at breakfast, and happily fetch booster seats for little princes and princesses. And if that’s not enough to make you feel at home, perhaps the stylish rooms and common spaces will, designed as they are to offer a true sense of place. Modern sculptures and paintings by living Thai artists, and subtle design nods to the country’s silk-making history and garments worn by traditional Thai dancers, delight at every turn. —Matt Ortile

It feels like you might be in London when you're at The Peninsula in Bangkok's Thonburi neighborhood, thanks in part to the British racing vehicles parked out front. But the hotel's custom tuk-tuk reminds you that you're in Thailand, and rich, warm toffee tones carry throughout the lobby and lounges. The space offers grand views over the Chao Phraya and the Thai river homes across the water. The Peninsula swimming pool is among the best in the city; there's no better way to beat the heat in this famously hot capital than by taking a dip right on the river. —J.A.

In a city where almost every high-end hotel brand has already made a mark, it takes something extra special to turn heads. Yet when Capella Bangkok finally opened after a seven-year tease, the city’s high-society set swooped in like magpies. Why? Capella’s first foray in Thailand is the only city hotel with villas right on the Chao Phraya River—multi-roomed retreats with private gardens and swimming pools lined with travertine marble. Suites in the main building—a blocky, low-slung affair with 101 rooms—come with plunge pools on their balconies, and the hotel tapped hot-shot chef Mauro Colagreco (of Mirazur in France) to head its signature coastal Mediterranean restaurant, Côte. Crystalline coupes of private-label Champagne accompany check-in, brunches, and turn-down service, but that’s as flashy as it gets. The rest feels decidedly subdued. Service is hushed but switched-on, and the spa eschews New Age treatments for humble, age-old healing practices (tok sen hammer massages, luk pra kob herbal compresses) inspired by the historic Thai-Chinese community just outside its gates. —C.S.

Compared with many of its rivals, this Bangkok stalwart doesn’t have a location that’s wildly convenient: The postcard sights need a boat transfer, and most top tables are more than a 30-minute taxi ride away. But for the legions of loyal fans, that’s the point. Pitched up on a lush riverside plot in the hushed Dusit district, The Siam feels like a portal to a bygone Bangkok. Even though it opened over a decade ago, it’s easy to imagine it as a plush playground for the city’s erstwhile big guns. You'd be hard-pressed to point friends to a lovelier lunch spot than the hotel’s Thai restaurant, set between the timeworn pillars of three ancient teakwood houses, where butlers in dressy black sarongs deliver the kind of classic Thai hospitality—lilting “sawadee ka” greetings and tables set with fresh orchids—that’s becoming harder to find. None of which is to say that the hotel is stuffy—there’s a tattoo parlor in the spa. —Chris Schalkx

Making its debut in 2025 as the second Andaz outpost in Thailand, Andaz One Bangkok is an urban escape that deftly balances its proximity to Bangkok’s largest green park with its connection to the city’s fast-paced energy. Set in the Lumphini neighborhood, it offers direct views of leafy Lumphini Park while also keeping guests within reach of the business and shopping areas nearby. Rooted in Thai art, local female artists shine throughout the hotel, giving the space the feel of a gallery. Social spaces, ranging from the lobby lounge to the rooftop restaurant, make this the perfect place to relax and connect with other travelers. —M.L.

Opened in August 2026, Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit marks the Fairmont brand's debut in Thailand. The hotel is a comfortable base for exploring Sukhumvit, with public transportation and the Em District within walking distance, while its on-site restaurants, bars, and outdoor pool give plenty of reasons to stay in. Families are welcome, with a kids club and family-friendly pool complete with a waterslide. The interiors are modern and luxurious without losing their warmth, with thoughtful touches like the discreet, tucked-away reception desk and an impressive glass chandelier that is the talk of the town. For a hotel that's only been open a couple of months, the service is exceptional and thoughtful; by the end of the first day, everyone knows your name, making this new hotel feel like a luxe, warm, and welcoming home. —M.L.

The first hotel from Curio Collection by Hilton to arrive in Thailand, Kromo is a colorful celebration of Bangkok’s heritage with a contemporary edge. Located on Sukhumvit Road between Phrom Phong and Asoke, this 28-floor property is not what it seems from the outside; a modern black façade greets you at first glance, but once inside, a youthful pink-hued space opens up, with the hotel's lobby restaurant and bar just steps away. The hotel's design concept takes inspiration from a phrase in Bangkok's ceremonial Thai name, which translates to “The City of the Nine Gems,” brought to life in the creative social space Vilah (modeled after the chrysoberyl gem) and at the rooftop pool (designed after the zircon gem). Kromo sits at the foot of EM District, where three distinct shopping centers cater to every type of traveler. Across the way is one of Sukhumvit's most loved green parks for those needing a dose of nature and the occasional turtle sighting. —M.L.

The Dusit Thani Bangkok is in a class of its own, having first opened its doors five decades ago as one of the most glamorous and luxurious hotel experiences in Thailand. Following a full renovation, it reopened in 2024 with a refreshed Thai-inspired look while still holding on to the same warm, local hospitality that built its reputation. Located within the upper echelons of Silom, the hotel overlooks Lumphini Park, promising inescapable views from every room. Centrally located between the Chao Phraya River and the shopping mecca of Sukhumvit, guests have close access to everything from a rooftop garden to a retail center filled with local shops and popular dining spots. The property is also kid-friendly, with a kids club and cultural activities that are actually fun for little ones. —M.L.

Kimpton Maa-Lai manages to provide something not every large hotel can: a stay that’s both intimate yet connected to the city's lively social scene. The modern, stark façade is a contrast to what you’ll find inside—buzzing cafés, intimate bars, rare green space tucked into Bangkok's urban jungle, and spacious rooms with nature-inspired touches and Thai decor. On-site, there are six dining options, from a Michelin-starred restaurant to a moody bar. Plus, as a Kimpton, the hotel is pet-friendly; kids and adults of all ages will love spotting furry friends roaming the lobby with their owners. Located within a hip retail and dining village and just a few minutes from the rows of shopping centers along Sukhumvit Road, there’s much to do at your fingertips. —Megan Leon

The Ritz-Carlton's entry into Bangkok brought with it a serene stay in an evolving corner of the city with easy access to major sites and the brand's signature impeccable service. It sits on the One Bangkok campus, a $3 billion development with hotels, office buildings, condos, a massive shopping mall, an entertainment complex, and plenty of public art and outdoor space. Guest rooms begin on the eighth floor and go up to 24, half of which have balconies or outdoor space. Room types start at a Deluxe King or Deluxe Double, many with stand-alone tubs and walk-in rain showers, and expand up to The Ritz-Carlton Suite, a two-bedroom with a massive walk-in closet, dining room, bar, Lumphini Park views, and lounge access. Be sure to book a meal at Duet by David Toutain (whose eponymous Paris restaurant has two Michelin stars); his team serves modern French cuisine in the form of a seasonal tasting menu heavy on seafood, fresh vegetables, and ornate presentation. —Madison Flager

Romantic and right on the river, Amdaeng fits the bill if you want to relax and recharge away from the frenzy of the city. Inside, find interiors that include alligator-print leather sofas, a red swimming pool, bathtubs with chrome lion feet, Thai tilework, and Chinese antiques. Directly outside the hotel, wander the canals of the Thonburi District, crossing small bridges, visiting Buddhist spirit houses, and seeing the big banyan trees. Here, you'll get a taste of everyday life in Bangkok. You’ll find neighbors catching up curbside over noodles, and true hidden-gem restaurants. This hotel feels like a hidden discovery, tucked down an alley alongside a canal. —Jenny Adams

There’s no hotel quite like Bangkok Publishing Residence in the city, with its antique typewriters and cabin-chic rooms. Evoking the image of a Mad Men daydream, it's a time capsule of a former publishing heyday. With a treasure trove of antiquities and a lobby that preserves the building’s former life as a weekly series publisher, you won’t find anything like it anywhere. The owner inherited her grandfather’s printing house, restoring and reimagining it as a character-driven hotel with only eight rooms and miles of soul. If this is the first hotel you experience in Bangkok, it’s going to set a very high bar. But it can be tough to snag a stay, as this place sees frequent return guests. —J.A.

The Anantara Siam Bangkok Hotel, which draws a fashionable crowd of international travelers, is a verdant sanctuary in the retail jungle. Much to the delight of those staying here, the property has a stronger resort vibe than many hotels in this area, with tropical landscaping, a central swimming pool, gorgeous rooms, and old-world Thai details. It also offers some of the only terrace rooms in town; they come with adjoining gardens where you can sit out on a private patio. —J.A.

The Park Hyatt Bangkok has the feel of an art gallery, where striking design elements surprise you, but nothing gets in the way. You're pointed to the hotel entrance by a series of discreet signs in gold lettering, then elevators take you to the beautiful 10th-floor lobby, decorated in cream and white and accented with simple but bold artwork. Even the sleek, sculpted reception desk looks like modern art. The rooms are beautiful, and the bathrooms feel like spas. Penthouse Bar & Grill, which spans three upper floors of the building, was designed by the famous New York firm of AvroKo. The idea was to turn one seamless space into five separate venues with marble, ebony, and gold accents, plus antique British stylings. —Audrey Phoon

What are the best areas to stay in Bangkok?

The riverside neighborhoods of Rattanakosin and adjacent Banglamphu are a great starting point, with their famous temples like Wat Po, plus the Grand Palace complex, old forts, sunny parks, and the backpacker zone of Khao San Road. If you’re a fan of stiff drinks and sharp suits, visit Thonglor—often compared to Brooklyn—where a heavy Japanese expat community has resulted in great omakase joints, cool vintage purveyors, and a collection of high-end tailors. This is also the city’s nexus for hot new cocktail spots.

Chinatown’s tiny lane, Soi Nana, gets global nods for its handful of craft libation and beer bars, all cutting-edge but delightfully ramshackle. This neighborhood could take you a week to fully explore, jam-packed as it is with 300-year-old Taoist temples, darling coffee houses, serious dim sum, great shopping, and a maze of old-world food markets. If shopping and art are on the agenda, head to Siam, where you’ll find the city’s largest art museum, as well as a range of malls.

What’s the best way to get around Bangkok?

Bangkok’s traffic is infamous. However, if you plan accordingly, it’s hardly an issue. In the riverside neighborhoods and Chinatown, it’s easy to walk. The streets are flat and the sites are close together. Along Sukhumvit Road—the main artery that connects the mid-city neighborhoods like Thonglor, Siam, Prom Phong, and Sathorn—you can use the BTS SkyTrain. It’s simple to follow English maps, posted nearly everywhere, with colored lines and an easy ticket-purchasing process. This raised train runs every day from 6 a.m. to midnight and has three separate lines that connect huge portions of the city. Finally, make sure to hop in a tuk-tuk. Thailand’s famous rickshaw vehicles provide a fun, exhilarating way to experience the city.

I recommend visiting Bangkok for a minimum of three days, which will give you time to explore a few temples, get a taste of local street food in Chinatown, squeeze in a foot massage, and spend time gallery hopping at the new Dib Bangkok art museum or shopping at one of Bangkok’s many malls.

The best time to visit is from November through February, when the monsoon season has ended and the cooler season arrives—and by cooler, I just mean a degree or two less than usual.

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

10 Best Subscription Boxes for Kids (2026): STEM, Books, Clothes, Snacks, and More

📅 2018-11-24  |  Read Source →

If you’re shopping for a unique gift idea this holiday season, these subscription boxes for kids are something young ones of all ages will get to enjoy not just on Christmas morning, but all year long. It can be something you know they’ll love, or just never-ending toys if it’s one of those ages where their interests are changing by the minute.

We’ve had all kinds of kid and parent testing with this guide. I’m the parent of a 4-year-old, while former WIRED senior editor Adrienne So tested kids subscription boxes with an 8-year-old and 10-year-old. Our latest recommendations were tested with a baby. Really, there’s no limit on what age these boxes can delight and teach. After years of testing, these are our favorites.

Looking for more kid gear? Don’t miss our guides to the Best STEM Toys, Best Baby Gear, and Best Kid Backpacks. Shopping for a parent? We’ve got gift guides for moms, dads, and new parents alike.

Updated November 2026: We’ve rearranged our top picks and updated our notes about Kiwi Crate and Lovevery’s subscription boxes. We also updated pricing information for all of our recommendations.

Kiwi Crate has a series of crates designed for different age groups, from the Panda Crate (designed for babies and toddlers under three) to the Maker and Eureka Crates aimed at 12 and up. Each box comes with a themed activity designed for its age group.

I tested out a Koala Crate, designed for ages three to six, with my 4-year-old son, and he's been loving every piece of it. It was themed around dinosaurs with a dinosaur bone dig kit and a dinosaur dress-up set, both of which my son loves. The dress-up set was four accessories (a headband, two hand pieces, and a tail on a belt) that made it easy for a variety of sized kids to use, and I loved that the dig kit came with two different dinosaur bone sets that fit into a little puzzle cut-out board when he's done digging.

Kiwi Crate's boxes come every month (except for the Panda Crate, which comes every two months), and the cost stays the same as you move through the different age groups—you won't be hit by a sudden price increase when your kid is older. —Nena Farrell

When I became a parent, I felt like I had a million things to do, or research how to do. My Lovevery subscription at least let me stop worrying about getting “the right toys.” While I only used it for the first 10 months, most of the toys were a huge hit with my kiddo. Not only did each kit include a variety of toys, each one included an entire booklet for parents about early childhood development, and how each toy was meant to stimulate your child.

During the first two months, my kiddo would stare at the high contrast cards of The Looker Play Kit constantly. Months three and four were dominate by the silicone teether toy and soft book inside The Charmer Play Kit. The stacking cups of The Inspector Play Kit quickly became (and remain) bath toys. While I cancelled after about 10 months, I would recommend this to any new parent with an empty toy shelf. —Harry Rabinowitz

Lalo’s Play Boxes are another good option made for the littlest people in our lives. There are 10 different boxes of toys that are designed for different months within the first two years of a kiddo’s life, starting at the zero-to-12-month infant stage. It’s available both as a subscription or a one-off purchase of a specific developmental window, such as three to four months or 16 to 18 months. You can even add it to a registry on Babylist.

The toys are beautifully made with nontoxic materials. I tried out two different Lalo Play Boxes and was happy to see that my son was usually interested in at least three of the items from each box (a good ratio for a toddler). Most of the toys we tested were made of wood, like the wooden blocks he likes to knock over from the 19 to 21 month box and the drum he plays from the 13 to 15 month set. I’m honestly jealous of how pretty some of the toys are and regularly resist the temptation to steal the cute Stacking Rocket for my bedside table.

Each box comes with a little Play Guide that describes how the toys are meant to be used and how they stimulate their specific age group. The booklet also gave tips on how to use the toys as your kid gets older, too. —Nena Farrell

My kids are 8 and 10, and they are obsessed with puzzles of all kinds. This is great because they are at the age when they need to practice reading, and there are only so many times you can force them to reenact The Lord of the Rings trilogy. The classic children's publisher Highlights also offers a few different reading and activity boxes, in addition to the iconic magazine. My kids and I tried the I Can Read book club ($13/month) and the Puzzlemania subscription ($4/month). Puzzlemania was delightful.

Each puzzle book is 32 pages and has a wide variety of puzzles, including sticker puzzles, word searches, Mad Libs–style storytelling, and riddles. We spent several afternoons filling in sticker puzzle pieces and playing the Highlights version of Sudoku. They both loved this puzzle pack so much that I bought the Highlights Great Big Book of Really Hard Puzzles ($8), which I'm anticipating will keep them occupied for at least one weekend trip or two. —Adrienne So

This is the best box. Kids need to snack every day anyway, so you might as well read and learn while you're at it. My kids tear into the Universal Yums snack box like a small pack of very tiny wolves. You can choose a small, medium, or large box, and it includes an informative booklet, games, and trivia.

Food is a great way to learn about geography and different cultures. Every month, my kids and I open the box, look at a globe, and do a lot of Googling. We have liked several foreign candies enough to start ordering them separately on Amazon. Even when the snacks aren't a hit—I got the salted truffle French fries all to myself—my kids always try them and ask a lot of questions about why a country is called the Kingdom of Butterflies and when we can visit. —Adrienne So

Cooking and baking subscription boxes are some of the best subscription boxes I've tried. Feeding kids every day is a chore, and I welcome any way to get some variety, even meal-delivery kits. Bake Eat Love is the first kit I was just as excited to try as my kids.

That said, the Bake Eat Love boxes are probably best suited for an older age group, with slightly more sophisticated palates. We tried the sampler box with tiramisu cupcakes. While I love the light, fluffy texture of tiramisu and the innovative recipe, my son was perturbed to find that a cupcake he assumed was chocolate tasted more like Mommy's coffee. The kit does include a few prepackaged ingredients, but as with most cooking and baking sets, you do have to have a basic set of cooking utensils and a few ingredients that might require an extra shopping trip, like mascarpone. —Adrienne So

Alternatives: I have gifted several Raddish Kids cooking club subscriptions to nieces and nephews. The recipes are extremely easy for little kids to follow (my children particularly loved making pretzels), and the included tiny utensils are adorable and perfect for tiny hands (and for moms who just like using tiny things). We also tried Eat2Explore, which was founded by a graduate of the French Culinary Institute. Each box features fun tools, nonperishable seasonings, recipe cards, and educational booklets from different countries. The salmon teriyaki was not the right pick for a child who has described fish as smelling like “stinky garbage,” but he did love using the included chopsticks. This is a fun, relatively affordable way to try to expand a kid's picky palate. —Adrienne So

This is coming with a big disclaimer: CrunchLabs, the company founded by former NASA engineer and YouTuber Mark Rober, says that its Hack Pack is for people over 14 years old. However, my 8-year-old put it together with minimal help in an afternoon, although it did take him much longer than the 60-minute estimated time for a teenager. ("Why are you so worried, Mama?" he admonished me when I showed skepticism. "The drawings show you exactly what to do.") Each box has a robot to assemble that illustrates a STEM principle, complete with a battery and an Arduino microcontroller. You can also use video instructions, but the drawings in the included manual were clear and big enough that we could put it together without the help of the internet.

Our box had the infrared turret to illustrate the principle of infrared communication. My 8-year-old was thrilled, hiding it and using the infrared remote to ambush his sister with a barrage of foam darts. You can also unlock a web-based coding console to hack the robot by locking out other users. It's expensive, but the price-per-payoff valuation is worth it—the STEM principle it illustrated was interesting, the build process was engaging without being frustrating, and the project itself was very fun. Do note that the subscription is annual, with different pay frequency options. —Adrienne So

CrunchLabs is great, but it is generally aimed at older kids. The Creative Kit subscription I tried is aimed at 6- to 10-year-olds, the youngest of the brand's offerings.

I'm shocked at how well-thought-out these kits are. The Creative Kit's we tried were the Ice Cream Stand and the Architect's Treehouse. The morning after the crates were assembled, both kiddos begged to get more. Even after my 8-year-old son had put together the tiny ice cream stand, he continued to play with it all afternoon. It comes with delightful little accessories, like moldable ice cream in different “flavors” (colors), little toppings, and tiny cones and cups. (I was offered a tiny scoop of “Super Strawberry Smash.”) Unlike most tie-dye or pinwheel kits, the Creative Kit encourages play long after the craft has been completed. My 10-year-old likes these better than the Kiwi Crates because “it's like building a tiny town!” —Adrienne So

My third-grader is a voracious reader. But it took him a few years and some hurdles to get to this point. In that time, the Lovevery Reading Skill Set was invaluable. These books and games are a complete homeschool reading curriculum aimed at pre-K through the second grade, but we used them as supplementary materials. Each set comes with three separate components: lovely, sturdy games; a few books; and parent course materials to explain both. You can buy an entire set together, or get a bi-monthly subscription, and there's three sets for different age groups.

The set was particularly crucial for my son during the second grade years. I particularly liked that the skill set addressed common errors and advanced vowel rules. It is really hard to remember what the letter “e” does in a word! My son found the board game to be very fun, like Chutes & Ladders but for word play. It was almost a disappointment when we realized, at the end of the summer, that he could actually read perfectly. —Adrienne So

As my kids have gotten older, shopping for their clothes has become more and more difficult. One child has sensory issues. He hates stiff or tight fabrics, clothes that are too fuzzy, certain colors, and all jackets. The other is a budding fashionista who is on a running team and dances and needs workout clothes, baggy jeans, or whatever else happens to not be in her closet at the moment. Whenever I find a sweatshirt they will wear, Target immediately discontinues it and my cycle of living hell continues.

Stitch Fix will cure what ails you, and you can start or stop your subscription as needed. You enter your child's age and size; color preferences and patterns to avoid; themes that they like; features to avoid (no crop tops); activities they like; and most importantly, budgets for every category. Stitch Fix sends you a box and you and your child keep what you like and send back the rest. You'll buy the individual items you like, and will pay a base $20 styling fee to get the box. I tested the box with my 10-year-old, and both of us liked the new picks. I was able to easily get an assortment of athletic clothing for her, as well as a cloud sweater she adores. This is an easy way to update wardrobes for kids who grow out of everything instantaneously and are really hard to shop for. —Adrienne So

Keke Pouch Subscription for $40: Kids are small factories of chaos. The constant stream of worksheets, drawings, and crafts is great for encouraging creativity and hand-eye coordination, but every surface in our house is perpetually cluttered. Rather than contributing to the mess, the Keke (Keep Every Kid Engaged) bag keeps every item organized. This frankly adorable, durable, handled bag has four activities in separate pouches that clip into binder rings, and extra storage pockets for masks or hand sanitizer. Every 12 weeks, the Keke subscription sends three new activities in new pouches to swap out. (You need to buy the bag separately.) Even though the activities are aimed at 3- to 6-year-olds (and some, like a simple puzzle, were too easy even when my son was 5), I love these bags for travel. I’ve been experimenting with different travel organizers to hold all my kids' markers, stickers, and card games for travel, and the Keke Bag is the best I’ve seen yet. —Adrienne So

Lingo STEM Subscription Box for $40: Lingo was founded by Aisha Bowe, a former NASA scientist, and is intended to bring STEM skills to children who may have been underexposed. That description does not precisely apply to my 7-year-old, but he nevertheless enjoyed this kit. We tried In the Driver's Seat ($75), which teaches you how to build a backup sensor for a car. Mileage will vary, and the kit is technically aged for sixth to 12th graders. However, my son and I found it easy to follow along once we figured out how to log in to the Lingo portal and access all the videos on his iPad. We followed the video instructions in the portal to learn how to build circuits on a breadboard using lights and resistors, and program to turn the lights on and off. I particularly like that it doesn't purport to teach children coding via puzzle pieces or blocks but uses an actual circuit board and a real programming environment. Lingo also offers teacher support if you get stuck. However, I should note that while the kit contains all the hardware components you need to build the sensor, you will need your own iPad or laptop to access the videos and instructions. —Adrienne So

Literati Gift Book Box for $63: If you and your family are struggling to find reading material for your required 20 minutes of reading per day for school (that's not Wings of Fire over and over again), I highly recommend a book subscription. We paid for a Literati subscription until its curation system worked against them. Literati offers book clubs that take newborn children up to their teens. Literati will send your child five books each month. Return any books you don't like and pay Amazon's list price for the rest. Every book was a hit, and each kid had to have every book in every box. For the sake of my wallet and our already-groaning bookshelves, I had to stop the subscription. You can gift a subscription or a one-time, age-appropriate theme box with a card, personalized stickers, and artwork. It's a great way to expose your children (and yourself!) to wonderful new works of art or literature without dragging them to a bookstore. —Adrienne So

Sketchbox Monthly Basic Box for $25: Art supplies—drawing, painting, pastels—are the delight of my family's life. SketchBox is a monthly box, and each month has a theme that's put together by an artist. My daughter's charcoal box was assembled by mixed media artist Nikoli Shaver and included a graphite starter kit, a small pack of media-appropriate paper, an eraser, charcoal pencils, and more. This box has an amazing value—the Nitram starter kit alone costs $16, and my 10-year-old spent several days sketching, tapping, and blending. If you're unsure of where to start with watercolor or oil pastels and find wandering Blick's aisles intimidating, these boxes are a great place to start. You can get a basic box for $25 or a premium one for $35, which has a higher-quality selection plus a piece of art to inspire you. —Adrienne So

Stickii Club Sticker Subscription for $12: My kids' appetite for stickers is endless. I find them constantly, on the mirrors in our house, on their school planners and water bottles, and occasionally stuck to the back of my chair or in the car. Stickers are also an accessible way of supporting independent artists. Maybe you can't buy a painting or a T-shirt, but a sticker only costs a few dollars and you can display it everywhere. For $12 a month, Stickii Club offers three different sticker styles—Cute, Vintage, or Pop—along with a storage sleeve and three stationery items, like a notepad, card, or stamp. The club works with independent artists and illustrators (no AI-generated art yet) to produce sheets of original designs. We tried the Pop subscription. These stickers are marvelous. There's a huge variety in the sheets sent. Some are vinyl, some are transparent, but all are high quality and intricately detailed. The artist is also noted on each corner so we can look them up ourselves. My kids were delighted and traded them with each other like currency. I am now investing in Stickii folios (from $18) in the hopes that I can keep these just a little bit more organized (and sticking a few on my laptop while I'm at it). —Adrienne So

The Weekly Junior for $49: This has been a pretty news-heavy few years. Other parents may disagree with me, but my kids really want to know what's going on in the world around us—in a safe, understandable, kid-friendly way, of course. The Week Junior is aimed at 8- to 14-year-olds, and my 10-year-old can now read it herself. Every week, we cuddle on the couch while they look at pictures and pick out which current events to read about, like the Olympics, or whether apps should have likes. It's a great way to keep my kids informed without worrying that they'll hear swear words in my podcasts. —Adrienne So
